_howTo: This is the watchlist. To add an ETF, copy one of the blocks under 'etfs', change id/yahoo/market/currency,
choose its category and long-run proxy (what it invests in), and add pipeline/etf_info/<id>.json with its facts.
The next pipeline run downloads its full history. ASX symbols end in .AX on Yahoo.
category (the group the app shows it in): Australian shares, Global shares, Currency-hedged, Diversified, Bonds, Gold, US-listed.
Proxy series you can use: au_shares, us_shares, global_shares, intl_shares (outside the US), us_tech, au_bonds, us_bonds, cash_au, cash_us, gold.
Weights must add up to 1. 'hedged': true means the part is currency-hedged (no AUD/USD conversion).
proxyWarning (optional): one or two plain sentences on how rough the proxy is; copied into data/monthly.json.
trFrom (optional): 'listing' or a date, when the issuer confirms Yahoo's distribution records are complete from there (VGAD paid nothing before Jul 2016).

etfs.proxyWarning: Tracks developed markets outside Australia with ESG screens (some companies left out); developed-world shares overall stand in for it.
Tracks developed markets outside Australia with a carbon tilt (less in heavy emitters); developed-world shares overall stand in for it.
Before 2013 uses shares outside the US from Kenneth French's data, which are mostly developed markets (VEU also holds emerging markets). No data before 1975.
A concentrated ethical fund (about 200 large companies, more technology and no fossil fuels); developed-world shares overall are only a rough stand-in.
Ethical screens leave out some industries (e.g. fossil fuels, weapons); developed-world shares overall stand in for it.
Holds only 'quality' companies (high profits, low debt), so it can do better or worse than the whole developed market for years at a time; developed-world shares overall stand in for it.
A concentrated fund of about 40-50 US companies chosen by Morningstar; the whole US market stands in for it, so its real returns can differ a lot in any year.

No high-dividend share series exists, so Australian shares overall stand in. VHY holds about 70 higher-yielding companies (more banks and miners), so its returns can differ a lot from the whole market in any year.

No Australian listed property series exists, so Australian shares overall stand in. Listed property is bumpier than the whole market (it fell roughly three-quarters in 2007-09, versus about half for all shares), so proxy months understate its risk.
International bonds (21%, hedged) are approximated by US 10-year Treasuries (hedged). Small companies and emerging markets use developed-world shares as a stand-in.

International bonds (35%, hedged) are approximated by US 10-year Treasuries (hedged), which swing more with interest rates than VBND's mix of shorter government and company bonds. Small companies and emerging markets use developed-world shares as a stand-in.

International bonds (42%, hedged) are approximated by US 10-year Treasuries (hedged), which swing more with interest rates than VBND's mix of shorter government and company bonds. Small companies and emerging markets use developed-world shares as a stand-in.

No free long-run global bond series exists, so US 10-year Treasuries (hedged to A$) stand in. VBND's bonds are shorter (about 6 years' duration, versus about 8 for a 10-year Treasury) and include company and non-US government bonds, so the proxy swings more with interest rates.

Before 2008 (when its Yahoo prices start) uses the World Bank's monthly average gold price, converted to A$. Averages smooth the moves (about 10% less bumpy month to month than GOLD's real month-end prices) and only loosely match them month by month, though the long-run growth matched well (2008-2026: 9.3% a year real, 9.8% proxy).
